Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. For a nonempty block $B\subseteq I$, write $S_B=\prod_{i\in B}S_i$, $S_{-B}=\prod_{i\in I\setminus B}S_i$, let $p_{-B}:S\to S_{-B}$ be the coordinate projection, and define $\pi_{-B}(D):=\pi(p_{-B}^{-1}(D))$ for measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$.

Products and product sigma-algebras use the empty-product convention in [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: if $B=I$, then $S_{-B}$ is the one-point space $\{()\}$ with its trivial sigma-algebra.

A **proper full conditional kernel** for block $B$ is a supplied probability kernel $K_B:S_{-B}\to S_B$ such that for every product-measurable $C\subseteq S$ and every measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$,

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable

$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.

Expanding each squared term verifies the exponents, and multiplying the factors verifies the prefactors.

For any $c\in\mathbb R$, $s>0$, and Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, the diffeomorphism $T(t)=c+st$ in [F4] gives $\int_A g_{c,s}(z)\,dz=\int_{T^{-1}(A)}\phi(t)\,dt=N(c,s^2)(A)$ by [F5]. Thus each $g_{c,s}$ is a probability density. Applying [F6] to the first factorization in step 2.1 yields $m_Y(y)=\int p(x,y)\,dx=g_{m_Y,\sigma_Y}(y)$; the second factorization gives $m_X(x)=\int p(x,y)\,dy=g_{m_X,\sigma_X}(x)$. These marginal densities are finite and strictly positive at every real argument.

Apply [F7] to $p$ with Lebesgue reference measures and, for each updated coordinate, the supplied filler $N(0,1)$ from [F5]. Since both marginal densities in step 3.1 are finite and positive everywhere, the density formula is used on every conditioning fibre. For measurable $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, the first conditional kernel is $K_X(y,A)=\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,dx}{m_Y(y)}=\int_Ag_{a(y),s_X}(x)\,dx=N(a(y),s_X^2)(A)$, using the factorization in step 2.1 and density identification in step 3.1. Exchanging coordinates gives $K_Y(x,A)=N(b(x),s_Y^2)(A)$.
